extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially novelists and new/aspiring authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for plotting novel-length fiction, focusing on how to create depth and immersion by weaving multiple plotlines, using inner/outer journeys, viewpoint characters, and the 'broken narrative' technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple plot lines / the weave
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot has multiple story lines; a good story has at least two plots (outer and inner), and often additional plots (e.g., romantic or friendship plots).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visually the outer journey is only one line; if you write only the outer journey the tale feels thin and pointless. Weave multiple plots together to give a novel weight and substance. The author notes novels may have many intertwined plots (he mentions sometimes five or six viewpoint characters each with four or five plots, and even thirty plot lines integrated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner journey / character growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Include an inner journey for the protagonist — a plot line of growth that runs alongside the outer journey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inner journey shows personal growth as the protagonist stumbles and learns life lessons necessary for the outer journey's successful conclusion. Without a strong inner arc, the novel will feel underdeveloped even if the external plot is executed well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outer journey / classical plot elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct an outer plot line with recognizable structural beats (beginning, inciting incident, try/fail cycles, climax, denouement, validation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing 'plot line' the author refers to these standard elements; they form the visible, action-driven arc of the tale that should interlock with inner and other subplots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weave subplots tightly / integration of threads
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat subplots like threads; the tighter and more integrated the weave, the stronger the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subplots should be connected and reinforce each other. Include viewpoint and important non-viewpoint characters whose stories become woven together. Tight integration increases weight and substance; loose, unconnected subplots dilute impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple viewpoint characters and split narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ multiple viewpoint characters and intentionally split or alternate narratives to create complexity and scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tolkien splits Frodo/Sam from Merry/Pippin, and inserts other characters' narratives to expand the tale. Splitting the narrative and interleaving viewpoints allows many narratives to be woven into one powerful story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken narrative technique (introduce new narratives / break the flow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately 'break' a running narrative by introducing other stories or digressions to add dimension and complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites Milton Erickson's hypnotic 'Broken Narrative' technique and literary examples (Poe, Homer). Breaking the narrative can deepen reader engagement by shifting mental states; it's a technique to overload the conscious mind and force deeper processing. Use judiciously to enrich the story rather than confuse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the novel as interwoven short stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that a novel may be made up of interwoven short stories or be a short story in form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algis Budrys' point: dozens of short stories can be woven into a longer narrative. Plan subplots and episodes so each can stand as a coherent piece while contributing to the larger whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden scope beyond the protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the story begin before the protagonist enters it and extend beyond when they leave; involve more than just the protagonist in the tale's world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A compelling novel often influences the whole world it describes. Make scenes and subplots that show events outside the protagonist's immediate experience to convey a larger, richer setting and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overwhelm the conscious mind to create immersion
rubrics_metrics.description: To move readers into a deeply immersive ('theta') state, present enough narrative complexity that their conscious mind struggles to hold everything at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using multiple interleaved plots and broken narratives can overwhelm the conscious mind, forcing readers' subconscious to synthesize disparate elements and thereby feel as if they 'lived through' the tale. The goal is deep engagement and a sense of lived experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on a single storyline for a novel-length work
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on a single linear storyline to carry a novel; that tends to produce a thin, underdeveloped tale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even beautifully executed single plots often feel insubstantial at novel length. Instead, plan and weave additional threads (inner arcs, subplots, viewpoint strands) to build complexity, depth, and reader investment.
